strengths: Provides the first (to the authors' knowledge) provable last-iterate convergence guarantee to an exact Nash equilibrium of the unregularized general-preference alignment game, closing a real gap left by prior methods (IPO/SPPO which only average-iterate converge, and Nash-MD/INPO which converge only to a KL-regularized equilibrium lacking the 50% robust-alignment guarantee).

Nice unifying perspective: shows that many existing RLHF/preference-optimization algorithms (PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO) can be viewed as instantiations of the prox operator, making COMAL a practical black-box meta-algorithm that can wrap around existing implementations with minimal change.

Theoretical analysis is thorough, covering both the idealized exact-solve setting and a more realistic inexact-solve setting with explicit approximation-error requirements (Theorem 3), plus a linear convergence rate for the inner regularized-game solver (Theorem 2).

Clean, illustrative synthetic 3-action intransitive preference experiment convincingly visualizes the cycling/divergence of MWU-based methods versus the convergence of COMAL, well aligned with the theory.

LLM-based experiments are more extensive than prior comparable work (up to 42 iterations vs. 3 in INPO), and results consistently show COMAL achieving win rate strictly above 50% against all baselines and better stability (less degradation) at later iterations/final checkpoints.
weaknesses: LLM experiments are limited to a single relatively small model (Qwen2-1.5B) and a single dataset (UltraFeedback); it is unclear whether the benefits of COMAL persist at larger model scales or across different preference distributions/datasets.

The evaluation oracle (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) is used both for generating training preference data and for evaluation, which risks the reported win-rate improvements reflecting overfitting to the oracle's idiosyncrasies rather than genuine alignment quality; no human evaluation or independent GPT-4-based AlpacaEval score is reported.

The practical reference-policy update rule in COMAL (switching when the inner solver 'begins to converge or overfit') is heuristic and not clearly automated or theoretically justified, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns for the practical algorithm versus the idealized meta-algorithm.

The absolute magnitude of empirical gains is fairly modest (e.g., COMAL vs. INPO-Small around 51-57% win rate), and the pairwise win-rate tables are somewhat self-referential (comparisons mostly among the algorithms' own checkpoints) rather than benchmarked against strong external baselines or larger multi-turn/human-annotated benchmarks.

The theoretical guarantees rely on exact or near-exact computation of the prox operator; in practice this is approximated via finite-sample optimization of INPO-style losses, and the paper does not empirically verify how closely the practical implementation approximates the theoretical inexact-convergence conditions (e.g., required O(1/t^4) error rates).

Output length increases substantially for some methods (e.g., INPO-Large, Iter-IPO) which could confound win-rate comparisons if the preference oracle has length bias; the paper does not fully control for or discuss this potential confound in COMAL's reported gains.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important problem: existing algorithms for finding Nash equilibria under general (non-Bradley-Terry) preferences either diverge or only converge in an average-iterate sense or to a KL-regularized (not the true) equilibrium.

Clean theoretical contribution: COMAL is a natural application of the conceptual prox-method (Nemirovski) to the LLM alignment setting, and the paper provides a rigorous last-iterate convergence proof (Theorem 1), including an extension to approximate/inexact regularized-game solves (Theorem 3), which appears novel in this context.

The meta-algorithm perspective usefully unifies many existing preference optimization methods (DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO, PPO) as instances of computing a prox operator, which is conceptually clarifying and potentially useful for future algorithm design.

The synthetic 3-action intransitive preference game experiment is a clear and illustrative diagnostic that visually demonstrates cycling/divergence of MWU-based methods (DPO, IPO, SPPO) versus convergence of COMAL, matching the theory well.

The LLM-based experiments scale iterative training further than prior work (up to 42 iterations/7 rounds vs. 3 iterations in INPO), and show COMAL maintaining >50% win rate against all baselines at both best and final checkpoints, with a positive story about stability over many training rounds.
weaknesses: Single model/dataset evaluation: LLM experiments use only one small model (Qwen2-1.5B) and one dataset (UltraFeedback), with no exploration of larger/more capable models or diverse tasks, limiting evidence that findings generalize to realistic alignment settings.

The evaluation is entirely self-referential: the same preference oracle (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) is used both to generate training preference data and to evaluate win rates, and no external/human evaluation or standard benchmark score (e.g., MT-Bench, standard AlpacaEval with GPT-4) is reported, raising concerns about circularity/overfitting to the oracle rather than genuine alignment quality.

No hyperparameter search was done for COMAL itself, and the reference-policy update schedule in COMAL (switching from INPO-Small to a higher-η regime) appears to be manually/heuristically triggered based on observing INPO's performance plateau/overfitting rather than a principled or automatic stopping criterion, undermining the claim of a simple, easily-integrable meta-algorithm; it's unclear how this choice would be made without hindsight knowledge of INPO's trajectory.

Output length substantially increases for COMAL and other iterative methods (Figure 3), suggesting possible reward/preference-oracle hacking (verbosity bias) rather than genuine quality improvement; the paper does not control for length or verify win rates are not simply driven by length bias.

The core convergence guarantee (Theorem 1) assumes the Prox operator/inner regularized game is solved exactly, and even the inexact version (Theorem 3) requires the reference policy π* to have full support matching πsft and exponentially decreasing error tolerances (ε_t = O(1/t^4)) achieved via O(log t) inner iterations — assumptions that are difficult to verify or achieve in practice with neural network optimizers with non-convex losses and finite samples, making the practical relevance of the theory strained.

The comparison set of baselines, while covering major methods, does not include more recent or stronger iterative self-play baselines (e.g., DNO, Nash-MD, SPPO in the LLM setting) in the LLM experiments — only Iter-IPO and two INPO variants are compared against COMAL in Table 2/3, despite Table 1 listing more methods.

Win-rate margins in Table 2 (e.g., 50.00 to 55.9% against the closest competitor Iter-IPO) are modest, and no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported advantages are robust or within noise given LLM preference-oracle judgment variance.

The practical implementation of COMAL (Algorithm 4) requires manually chosen schedules for τ_t, η_t, and K_t across iterations, and the paper does not provide clear general guidance for setting these hyperparameters beyond the specific values used in this single experimental setting, limiting reproducibility and applicability to new settings.

The novelty of the core algorithmic idea is somewhat incremental: applying the well-known conceptual prox-method/proximal point framework (originally from Nemirovski 2004 and prior game-theory literature such as Perolat et al.) to LLM alignment is a relatively direct application rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic insight, and the paper explicitly acknowledges it is not proposing new optimization algorithms but rather a unifying perspective.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: existing methods for general-preference alignment either diverge in the last iterate or only converge to the Nash equilibrium of a KL-regularized (modified) game, losing the 50% robust-alignment guarantee. COMAL is the first, to the authors' knowledge, to provably achieve last-iterate convergence to an exact Nash equilibrium of the unregularized game.

Elegant unifying perspective: the paper shows that many existing RLHF/preference-optimization algorithms (PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO) can all be viewed as instances of computing a Prox operator, allowing COMAL to be implemented as a simple wrapper ('update the reference policy') around any of these methods with minimal code change.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 proves monotonic KL decrease and last-iterate convergence under exact regularized-game solutions, and this is further extended (Theorem 3, Appendix B.2) to the more realistic setting of approximate solutions with an explicit error-decay schedule — a level of rigor exceeding most prior work in this area.

Well-designed synthetic experiment with an explicit intransitive 3-action preference cycle clearly and visually demonstrates that MD/IPO/SPPO cycle indefinitely, DPO diverges to extreme deterministic policies, INPO converges but to the wrong (regularized) equilibrium, while COMAL alone converges cleanly to the true Nash equilibrium — providing clean, convincing validation of the theoretical claims.

LLM-scale experiments (Qwen2-1.5B on UltraFeedback, up to 42 iterations, 7 rounds) go well beyond the iteration budgets used in prior work (e.g., INPO only ran 3 iterations), and show COMAL achieving win rate >50% against every other baseline's best and last checkpoints, along with much better stability at the final checkpoint compared to INPO and iterative IPO, supporting the practical value of the reference-policy-update mechanism.

Clear, well-organized writing with a helpful comparison table (Table 1) situating COMAL relative to DPO/IPO/SPPO/Nash-MD/INPO along three key axes (general preference, last-iterate convergence, robust alignment), and thorough related-work coverage of both the alignment and game-theoretic optimization literatures.
weaknesses: The main LLM-based empirical validation relies on a single relatively small model (Qwen2-1.5B) and a single preference oracle (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) that is used both for training and evaluation, which raises potential concerns about overfitting/reward-hacking to this specific oracle; results might not generalize to larger models, other datasets, or GPT-4-based evaluation.

The win-rate improvements of COMAL over strong baselines like INPO-Small/Large in the LLM experiments are often modest (e.g., 51-56% in Table 2), and no variance/multiple-seed information is reported, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the observed advantage.

The practical implementation of COMAL (Algorithm 4) deviates somewhat from the idealized meta-algorithm: the reference-policy update timing is chosen heuristically ('when the first optimization step begins to converge or overfit') rather than via a principled stopping criterion, and only one inner solver (INPO) is actually tested in the LLM experiments, despite the paper's claim of broad compatibility with PPO/DPO/IPO/SPPO/REBEL/DRO.

Theorem 1's guarantee relies on Assumption 1 (existence of a Nash equilibrium with full support matching πsft), and the practical algorithm requires solving each regularized subgame to near-exactness (Theorem 3 requires εt = O(1/t^4)), which is computationally demanding and only loosely approximated in the practical implementation without an accompanying empirical accuracy verification of the prox-operator convergence.

The computational cost of the experiments (8 A6000 GPUs, ~5 hours per iteration, up to 42 iterations) is substantial, which may limit reproducibility and independent verification, and no wall-clock/computation cost comparison against baselines is provided despite this being a practical concern for the community.

strengths: Provides the first (to the authors' knowledge) provable last-iterate convergence guarantee to the exact, unregularized Nash equilibrium of the LLM alignment game, extending prior last-iterate results (Perolat et al., Abe et al.) that required exact solving of the regularized subgame to a more realistic approximate-solving setting (Theorem 3), which is a genuine technical contribution.

Offers a unifying 'prox operator' perspective that shows how many existing preference-optimization algorithms (PPO, GRPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO) can be used as sub-solvers within COMAL, making the meta-algorithm easy to integrate into existing pipelines with minimal code changes.

Strong empirical validation across multiple axes: a clean synthetic 3x3 intransitive preference game that visually and quantitatively demonstrates convergence versus divergence/cycling of baselines; large-scale LLM experiments on both Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B; additional experiments with a smaller Qwen2-1.5B model in the appendix for more training iterations.

Careful ablations addressing potential concerns, e.g., checking for 'alignment tax' via standard benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval) and independent evaluation via GPT-4-based AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard, showing COMAL does not significantly harm general capabilities.
Clear related-work positioning and honest discussion of concurrent work (Wang et al. 2025), with a fair theoretical comparison highlighting the paper's stronger (approximate-solution) guarantee.

Thorough appendix with proofs, additional algorithm instantiations (GRPO, SPPO, DRO, REBEL), and a candid limitations section acknowledging lack of convergence-rate guarantees under fixed regularization and reliance on possibly non-convex losses in practice.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea builds heavily on existing tools (Nemirovski's conceptual prox method, prior work by Perolat et al., Abe et al., Sokota et al.), and a closely related concurrent work (Wang et al. 2025) achieves similar last-iterate convergence via Magnetic Mirror Descent; the paper's novelty is somewhat incremental (mainly the approximate-solution analysis and LLM-scale demonstration) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.
No direct empirical comparison against the concurrent last-iterate convergent baseline (Magnetic Preference Optimization / Wang et al. 2025) is provided, despite it being the closest related work.

The evaluation protocol trains and evaluates against the same (mixture-of-BT) preference oracle, which, while following prior work for controlled comparison, may inflate or bias results since the model is essentially optimizing for the exact metric it is tested on; no human evaluation or independent stronger oracle is used to corroborate the general-preference win-rate claims.

Reported win-rate margins against baselines are often modest (many head-to-head win rates around 50-65%, with COMAL underperforming Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard), suggesting the practical benefit, while consistent, is not dramatic.

Hyperparameter schedules (when/how to switch regularization strength τ or η across outer rounds) appear to be tuned somewhat ad hoc per model/dataset, which could limit reproducibility and generality of the specific recipe used.

Several claimed instantiations of COMAL (with GRPO, SPPO, DRO, REBEL) are only presented algorithmically in the appendix without any empirical validation, so the breadth of applicability claimed in the abstract is not fully substantiated experimentally.

Theoretical guarantees remain asymptotic for the unregularized game (only a rate is given for the regularized subgame), and the paper acknowledges that obtaining a practical non-asymptotic rate for the outer loop remains open, limiting the practical predictive value of the theory for finite-iteration LLM training.

strengths: The extension of last-iterate convergence guarantees for the conceptual prox method to the setting where each regularized subgame is solved only approximately (rather than exactly, as in prior work by Perolat et al., Abe et al., Sokota et al.) is a genuine theoretical contribution with a non-trivial proof.

The paper provides a nice unifying perspective showing that many existing preference-optimization losses (DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO, PPO/GRPO) can be viewed as instantiations of the prox operator, which gives useful practical guidance on how to plug them into the COMAL meta-algorithm with minimal code changes.

The synthetic 3-action intransitive preference experiment clearly and convincingly illustrates the cycling/divergence behavior of MWU-based methods (iterative DPO/IPO, SPPO) and the constant equilibrium gap of KL-regularized methods (INPO), in contrast to COMAL's clean convergence.

Reasonably extensive empirical validation across multiple model scales (1.5B, 7B, 8B) and two base models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B), with additional sanity checks on standard academic benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval) and GPT-4-based AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard to check for alignment tax.
weaknesses: The core empirical claims rely on evaluating trained policies with the exact same preference oracle used during training/data generation; algorithms whose objective is literally to maximize win-rate under this oracle (as COMAL more directly targets the unregularized game's Nash equilibrium) are somewhat structurally favored in this closed-loop setup, which limits the strength of the 60%/56% win-rate claims as evidence of real-world alignment quality (the GPT-4-based benchmarks are only a secondary 'sanity check' and show more mixed results, e.g., COMAL losing to Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard).

The hyperparameter treatment across baselines is not obviously matched: COMAL is allowed an adaptively scheduled KL-regularization strength (η⁻¹ changed across rounds, reference policy reset schedule tuned), while several baselines are run with fixed regularization or only two discrete settings (small/large), making it hard to disentangle gains due to the theoretical algorithmic design versus gains due to extra tuning flexibility given specifically to the proposed method.

The core theoretical machinery (conceptual prox method / mirror-prox for last-iterate convergence in monotone/zero-sum games) is well established in the game theory literature, and a concurrent work (Wang et al. 2025) proposes an essentially analogous algorithm; the paper's main novel piece is the approximate-solution analysis, which is a meaningful but somewhat incremental extension rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The paper's own Limitations section acknowledges that the theoretical guarantees require solving the regularized subgame to a specified approximation error, but no such guarantee actually holds for practical non-convex neural network training, leaving a substantial theory-practice gap that is not empirically probed (e.g., no measurement of how close the practical inner-loop training gets to the assumed approximation level).

Empirical evaluation is confined to a single training dataset (UltraFeedback) and one synthetic 3-arm bandit example; there is no demonstration on other preference datasets or larger/more realistic intransitive-preference structures, limiting evidence of generality.

Some baselines (Iter-IPO, INPO) show instability/degradation after only 6-7 iterations, which is used to argue COMAL's superiority, but it is unclear whether this instability is an intrinsic property of those algorithms or an artifact of the specific (possibly suboptimal) hyperparameters chosen for them in this comparison.

strengths: Provides a genuinely novel theoretical result: last-iterate convergence to the exact (unregularized) Nash equilibrium of the alignment game, going beyond prior work that only guarantees average-iterate convergence or convergence to a KL-regularized (and thus different) equilibrium. The extension to approximate regularized-game solutions (Theorem 3) is a meaningful and non-trivial generalization over prior Conceptual-Prox analyses that require exact solves.

Strong and diverse empirical validation: a clean synthetic 3-action cyclic-preference game clearly visualizes divergence/cycling of DPO, IPO, SPPO and constant-gap convergence of INPO versus exact convergence of COMAL; and large-scale LLM experiments on two different base models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B) plus an additional 1.5B-scale study, all showing consistent win-rate improvements.

The meta-algorithm framing (unifying PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO, GRPO as prox-operator solvers) is conceptually valuable and practically useful, and the paper backs this up with concrete instantiations (Algorithms 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) showing the idea is not just abstract.

Careful experimental design choices: using a mixture-of-BT-models oracle to simulate non-transitive human preference, controlled train/eval oracle consistency, and supplementary evaluation on standard benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, AlpacaEval, Arena-Hard) to check for alignment tax/capability degradation.

Good ablation and discussion connecting theory to practice, e.g., the analysis of reference-policy update frequency and its effect on stability vs. performance ceiling, and honest limitations section discussing the gap between theory (relies on exact/approximate prox solves) and practice (non-convex neural losses).
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees (Theorems 1-3) are proven for exact or provably-approximable prox-operator computations, but in the LLM instantiation the sub-solver (e.g., INPO with neural nets) is a non-convex optimization with no such guarantee; the paper is transparent about this in the Limitations section but the practical algorithm therefore has no formal convergence certificate.

LLM-scale experiments compare mainly against DPO/IPO/Iter-IPO/INPO; other Nash-equilibrium-seeking baselines explicitly discussed in the related work (e.g., Nash-MD, Online IPO) are not included in the large-scale comparisons, which slightly weakens the empirical case that COMAL dominates all competing general-preference approaches in practice.

Win-rate margins over the strongest baseline (INPO) are sometimes fairly close to 50% (e.g., 56.8-64.2% depending on model/regularization variant), and hyperparameters (η, τ, schedule of reference updates) differ substantially across methods/models, making it harder to fully disentangle gains due to the algorithmic design versus tuning choices.

The evaluation protocol uses the same preference oracle for training data generation and for evaluation, which is a reasonable controlled-experiment design (as acknowledged, following prior work) but limits claims about generalization to genuinely held-out or human-judged preferences beyond the AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard sanity checks.

No empirical evaluation of the alternative last-iterate convergent methods discussed in the appendix (Mirror-Prox, Optimistic MWU) at LLM scale, leaving open how COMAL's specific proximal/reference-update design compares to these other convergent alternatives in practice.
